technique.how: Press slowly and deeply with the fingertips over the area of concern (or a remote quadrant), hold, then release abruptly while watching the patient's face. Pain on release greater than on pressure is rebound tenderness. Gentler equivalents: percussion tenderness, or pain on coughing or heel-drop.
technique.prerequisites: Explain the manoeuvre; give analgesia first (it does not abolish peritoneal signs); perform once, not repeatedly.
technique.contraindications: Avoid in an already rigid, obviously peritonitic abdomen where the manoeuvre adds only pain; prefer percussion or cough tenderness.

interpretation.positive_finding: Rebound (or percussion/cough) tenderness indicates parietal peritoneal inflammation; in RIF pain it is specific for appendicitis (spec 0.89, sens 0.82 in adults; pediatric LR+ 3.0).
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence lowers the probability of appendicitis (pediatric LR- 0.28) but does not exclude early, retrocaecal or pelvic appendicitis or peritonitis in the elderly and immunosuppressed.
interpretation.pitfalls: The classic release manoeuvre is painful and non-specific in anxious patients; percussion or cough tenderness gives similar information more gently. False negatives occur with steroids, advanced age, obesity and altered mental status.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: escalate to imaging and surgical review for suspected appendicitis/peritonitis; negative in low-risk patients supports observation, not discharge without follow-up.

estimates.population: 100 consecutive patients with right iliac fossa pain, median age 25 (range 4-81), UK surgical unit; 44 histology-proven appendicitis
estimates.reference_standard: Histology at operation; non-operated patients followed clinically
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.82/(1-0.89) = 7.45; LR- = (1-0.82)/0.89 = 0.20; from abstract sensitivity 0.82 and specificity 0.89
estimates.quote: Rebound tenderness proved to be sensitive (sensitivity 0.82), specific (specificity 0.89) and accurate (accuracy 86%).

estimates.population: Children <=18 years in whom appendicitis was suspected and evaluation undertaken; pooled from quality level >=3 studies
estimates.reference_standard: Surgical pathology, clinical observation or follow-up
estimates.quote: rebound tenderness triples the odds of appendicitis (summary LR, 3.0; 95% CI, 2.3-3.9), while its absence reduces the likelihood (summary LR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.14-0.55)

sources.citation: Wagner JM, McKinney WP, Carpenter JL. Does this patient have appendicitis? JAMA. 1996;276(19):1589-1594.
Golledge J, Toms AP, Franklin IJ, Scriven MW, Galland RB. Assessment of peritonism in appendicitis. Ann R Coll Surg Engl. 1996;78(1):11-14.
Bundy DG, Byerley JS, Liles EA, Perrin EM, Katznelson J, Rice HE. Does this child have appendicitis? JAMA. 2007;298(4):438-451.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a negative result to exclude peritonitis in elderly, immunosuppressed, steroid-treated, obese or obtunded patients, or in pregnancy where the appendix is displaced.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Generalised rebound with fever, tachycardia or hypotension indicates diffuse peritonitis: resuscitate and obtain immediate surgical review.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Rebound is examiner- and patient-dependent; the pediatric RCE reports only fair agreement, and percussion/cough tenderness are more reproducible alternatives.

extraction_notes: Adult estimate from Golledge 1996 abstract (PMC deposit has abstract only, so table location not available; LRs computed by extractor from abstract sens/spec). Pediatric pooled LRs from Bundy 2007 abstract. Wagner 1996 adult RCE LRs (rebound LR+ ~1.1-6.3 range) are not visible in the abstract or any reachable full text and were not entered. Alshehri 1995 (PMID 7588144) reports rebound sensitivity 94.7% but in patients already admitted with a diagnosis of appendicitis, so it was omitted as spectrum-biased.
